front: TC012: What is the minimum viable move?
back: State your boundary as a need you have, not as a complaint about what they did. One sentence. Then stop.

front: TC012: What is the core sequence?
back: Name what you need -> Not what they did wrong -> Invite the alternative.

front: TC012: What is the field tip?
back: Say it as your need, not their fault.

front: TC012: What is the strong version of: Passive: 'I am quite busy... I will try... I will see...'?
back: I cannot take that on. What I can do is X.

front: TC012: What is the strong version of: Blaming: 'You always ask me last minute'?
back: I need more lead time for this. I can commit to X if you can give me Y days.

front: TC012: What is the strong version of: Over-apologising: 'I am so sorry, I really wish I could...'?
back: I cannot do it. Here is what I can offer instead.

front: TC012: What is better than: 'You clearly think my time is worthless.'?
back: 'I need my evenings offline. I will reply first thing.'

front: TC012: What is better than: 'I probably can't... I mean, unless it is really important?'?
back: 'I cannot this week. If it can wait until Monday, I am in.'

front: TC012: What is better than: Five reasons, each inviting a rebuttal?
back: 'That does not work for me.' — and stop.

front: TC012: What are signs it is working?
back: People respect the boundary without excessive argument. You do not feel guilty after stating it. The relationship stays intact. You follow through on what you said you would not do.

front: TC012: When should you avoid this technique?
back: When the behaviour is so serious that a firm objection — not a politely framed boundary — is the right response. In safety-critical situations requiring immediate compliance rather than a collaborative conversation.

front: TC012: What is the best recovery line?
back: 'That came out as an accusation — I meant it as a limit. Let me re-say it.'
